title: 06. Memory, State & HITL: Day 16 — Human-in-the-Loop
summary: Fully autonomous agents are a fantasy for most real productivity tasks. You do not want an agent sending an email to a customer without your review; you do not want a draft report shipped without your edit.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Fully autonomous agents are a fantasy for most real productivity tasks. You do not want an agent sending an email to a customer without your review; you do not want a draft report shipped without your edit. **Human-in-the-loop (HITL)** is the design pattern where the agent pauses at a checkpoint, surfaces its work to a human, and waits for a decision: approve, revise, or abort. Today you will build two such systems, one in LangGraph (which has first-class `interrupt()` support) and one in Pydantic AI (which gives you `agent.iter()` for visibility plus plain Python `input()` for the human turn).

### Three HITL flavors

HITL designs cluster into three flavors. The first is **approval gates**: the agent produces a complete artifact (email, code change, payment) and the human either approves or rejects. The artifact ships only on approval. This is what most production HITL systems use because it is the simplest to reason about and the safest. The second is **interactive editing**: the human can edit the artifact directly (or supply feedback that the agent incorporates), and the loop runs until the human is satisfied or gives up. The third is **supervisory escalation**: the agent runs autonomously but escalates specific cases (low-confidence, high-stakes, ambiguous) to a human reviewer. Today's projects cover the first two flavors; the third is the natural extension you will build in production-grade days.

The key architectural decision in any HITL system is **where the pause happens**. Two options: pause inside the agent framework (LangGraph `interrupt()`) or pause in user code that wraps the agent (Pydantic AI + plain `input()`). Framework-level pauses give you persistence for free: the agent's state survives a process restart, so a human can review a draft hours later. User-code pauses are simpler but require you to handle persistence yourself if the human might be away for a long time. We will build one of each so you can feel the tradeoff.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
**Forgetting the checkpointer.** `interrupt()` requires a checkpointer. If you compile your graph without `checkpointer=...`, calling `interrupt()` will raise a runtime error. The checkpointer is what lets the graph remember where it was between `invoke()` calls. For production use SQLite or Postgres persisters; `MemorySaver` is fine for dev but evaporates when the process exits.

**Blocking `input()` in async code.** If your HITL runs inside `asyncio`, plain `input()` will block the event loop. Use `await asyncio.to_thread(input, "Prompt: ")` (or `aioconsole.ainput`) to keep the loop responsive. The same applies to any other blocking I/O you do at the human turn.

**Mistaking `state.next` for "interrupted."** In LangGraph, `state.next` lists queued nodes whether or not the graph is paused at an interrupt. Always check `state.tasks[*].interrupts` to distinguish "paused waiting for human" from "just hasn't been invoked again yet." Otherwise you will try to resume a graph that wasn't actually interrupted and get a confusing error.

**Losing the `thread_id`.** Every `invoke()` and `get_state()` call needs the same `config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": ...}}`. Change the thread_id and you get a fresh state — your draft and revision count will vanish. Treat the thread_id like a session id and pass it through consistently.

**`field_validator` order matters.** In Project 2, the validator recomputes `word_count` from `body`. If you swap the field order in the model (so `word_count` is validated before `body`), `info.data.get("body")` will be empty and the recomputation silently fails. Pydantic validates in field-declaration order; keep dependencies in order or use `model_validator(mode="after")`.

sections.title: Next: Day 17 — Advanced Workflows
sections.body: Tomorrow you build two complex multi-step workflows. The Daily Planner mixes LLM nodes and pure-Python deterministic nodes in one LangGraph. The Weekly Status Report Generator orchestrates multiple data-fetching tools inside a single Pydantic AI agent to synthesize one weekly report from seven days of activity.
